Now I have enough material to compile the commentary. Let me assemble the notes verse by verse.

---

# Matthew 12:1–25 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## v. 1 — *At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry and began to pick the heads of grain and eat them.*

- **The setting:** Jesus and His disciples were likely walking to a synagogue for Sabbath worship. The fields contained either barley or wheat, and harvest had begun (Luke calls it "the first Sabbath after the second," i.e., the first Sabbath after the second day of Passover when the sheaf of firstfruits was offered). The disciples were hungry, probably because they had not yet eaten breakfast, and morning prayers in the synagogue customarily preceded eating. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/12.htm)

- **Gleaning was not stealing.** Deuteronomy 23:25 permitted travelers to pluck grain by hand for immediate consumption. The issue was exclusively the Sabbath. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

- **Poor and humble circumstances.** Spurgeon notes that Jesus, who fed multitudes miraculously, did not use that power to feed His own followers. "He left them till they did what poor men are forced to do to supply a little stay for their stomachs." (StudyLight/Spurgeon: https://www.studylight.org/library/charles-spurgeon/gospel-of-the-kingdom/35.html)

- **Rabbinical rules made it a violation.** In the eyes of the Pharisees, plucking grain counted as reaping, rubbing it as threshing, blowing away the chaff as winnowing, and eating it as preparing food — four Sabbath violations in one mouthful. The ancient rabbinic saying noted: "The rules about the Sabbath…are as mountains hanging by a hair, for Scripture is scanty and the rules are many." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

---

## v. 2 — *When the Pharisees saw this, they said to Him, “Look, Your disciples are doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath.”*

- **Pharisees as watchers.** These Pharisees were likely among those who had come from Jerusalem to observe and accuse Jesus (cf. Luke 5:17). They had already been offended at His claims to forgive sins and His eating with tax collectors and sinners. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

- **They appealed to the Teacher, not the disciples.** The charge was directed at Jesus: if He was a rabbi, He was responsible for His disciples' conduct. Gill notes the Pharisees expressed it "with astonishment, and indignation." (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/12.htm)

- **Maimonides codified this interpretation:** "He that reaps on the Sabbath, though never so little, is guilty. And to pluck the ears of corn is a kind of reaping." (Dummelow via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/matthew-12.html)

---

## vv. 3–4 — *Jesus replied, “Have you not read what David did when he and his companions were hungry? He entered the house of God, and he and his companions ate the consecrated bread, which was not lawful for them to eat, but only for the priests.”*

- **First defense: the example of David (1 Samuel 21:1–6).** David, fleeing Saul, came to Nob where the tabernacle was. Famished, he asked Ahimelech the priest for bread; only the showbread (bread of the Presence) was available — twelve loaves placed fresh each Sabbath, which by law (Leviticus 24:5–9) could be eaten only by priests. David took it and gave it to his men. Scripture never condemns David for this. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/12.htm; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

- **Jesus' argument is an *a fortiori* (lesser to greater) argument.** If David, a mere man, could in a case of urgent need set aside a ceremonial ordinance — and the high priest himself assented — and Scripture does not condemn him, how much less can the disciples be condemned for a far lighter act? (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm; Calvin via CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/study/Matthew_12:1-8)

- **Why this incident was a valid defense:** (1) It concerned eating; (2) it probably occurred on the Sabbath (the showbread was changed on the Sabbath, Leviticus 24:8); (3) it concerned not only David but his followers as well. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

- **Jewish tradition agreed with Jesus' logic.** Gill cites rabbinic sources acknowledging that "danger of life drives away the Sabbath" and that in cases of extreme hunger, the showbread could be eaten even by non-priests. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/12.htm)

- **The principle:** human need overrides ceremonial ritual. As Ellicott puts it, "When positive commands and necessities involving the good of man come into collision, the latter, not the former, must prevail." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

---

## v. 5 — *“Or haven't you read in the Law that on the Sabbath the priests in the temple break the Sabbath and yet are innocent?”*

- **Second defense: the priests' Sabbath work.** The priests were commanded to offer double sacrifices on the Sabbath (Numbers 28:9–10): slaying victims, kindling fires, lifting animals onto the altar, changing the showbread — all of which involved labour that, in any other context, would "profane" the Sabbath. Yet the Law declared them blameless because this was temple service. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/12.htm; Bridgeway: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/matthew-12.html)

- **The rabbinic principle:** "There is no prohibition in the sanctuary; that which is forbidden to be done on the Sabbath is lawful to be done in the sanctuary." (Gill, quoting Jewish sources: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/12.htm)

- Barclay notes that "The Temple ritual always involved work…This work was actually doubled on the Sabbath, for on the Sabbath the offerings were doubled" (cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/).

---

## v. 6 — *“But I tell you that something greater than the temple is here.”*

- **The staggering claim.** Jesus declares Himself — or His presence — greater than the temple. The Greek adjective is neuter in the best manuscripts ("something greater"), and Jesus may have accompanied it with a gesture toward Himself, as in John 2:19 ("destroy this temple"). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

- **What the temple lacked, Jesus is.** The temple in Jesus' day no longer had the ark of the covenant, the Shekinah glory, the sacred fire from heaven, or the Urim and Thummim. Yet Jesus embodied the presence of God — He was God made flesh. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

- **The logic:** If the temple and its service excused priests from blame for Sabbath work, how much more does the presence of One greater than the temple excuse His disciples? (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/12.htm; Calvin via CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/study/Matthew_12:1-8)

---

## v. 7 — *“If only you had known the meaning of 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice,' you would not have condemned the innocent.”*

- **Third defense: Hosea 6:6.** Jesus had already quoted this verse in Matthew 9:13. God prefers acts of compassion and mercy over ritual observances. The Pharisees had inverted the two: they elevated sacrifice (ceremonial law) above mercy (moral duty). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

- **The disciples were "guiltless."** Jesus pronounces them innocent — not because they technically obeyed the Pharisees' rules, but because mercy toward hungry men is never a sin. Matthew Poole observed: "Where two laws in respect of some circumstance seem to clash one with another, so as we cannot obey both, our obedience is due to that which is the more excellent law." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

- **Calvin's reading:** Jesus here teaches that "the ceremonies of the Law are not violated where there is no infringement of godliness." (Calvin via CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/study/Matthew_12:1-8)

---

## v. 8 — *“For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.”*

- **The climactic claim.** This is the fourth and most sweeping argument: Jesus, as the Son of Man (a Messianic title from Daniel 7:13), has authority over the Sabbath itself. He is not merely an interpreter of Sabbath law; He is its Lord, with power to dispense with and even abrogate it. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/12.htm; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

- **A claim to deity.** Only God could be Lord of what God instituted. Jesus claims the same authority that instituted the Sabbath at creation. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

- **Ellicott notes the title "Son of Man" is significant:** What Jesus does, He does "as the representative of humanity, acting, as it were, in its name, and claiming for it as such what He thus seems at first to claim for Himself." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

- **Mark 2:27 adds "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath."** Bridgeway connects this: "People are more important than the Sabbath. The Sabbath was given for people's benefit, not for their discomfort." (Bridgeway: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/matthew-12.html)

---

## v. 9 — *Moving on from there, Jesus entered their synagogue.*

- **Not necessarily the same Sabbath.** Matthew and Mark give the impression it was the same day, but Luke 6:6 states it was "another Sabbath." Jesus continued attending synagogue faithfully despite escalating opposition — "Jesus set the example of attending public worship." (Spurgeon, cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

- **"Their synagogue"** — probably the synagogue of the Pharisees whom He had just reproved, likely in Capernaum. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

---

## v. 10 — *And a man with a withered hand was there. In order to accuse Jesus, they asked Him, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?”*

- **The condition:** "Withered" (Greek: "dry") suggests a paralysed, shrunken hand, perhaps the right hand (Luke 6:6). According to the apocryphal "Gospel of the Hebrews," the man was a mason (stone-worker) who used his hands for his living. (Utley via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/matthew-12.html; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/12.htm)

- **The trap.** The Pharisees' casuistry permitted medical treatment on the Sabbath only when life was in danger (Mishnah Yoma 8:6). A chronic, non-life-threatening condition like a withered hand did not qualify. They anticipated that Jesus would heal the man and thereby give grounds for a formal accusation before the local tribunal. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm; Constable via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/matthew-12.html)

- **They expected Jesus to heal.** Whedon observes the irony: "They did not doubt that he was about to work a miracle; they expected it." Their aim was to argue that Jesus' miracles were contrary to divine law and therefore immoral — laying groundwork for the charge that His power was demonic. (Whedon via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/matthew-12.html)

---

## vv. 11–12 — *He replied, “If one of you has a sheep and it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will he not take hold of it and lift it out? How much more valuable is a man than a sheep! Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.”*

- ***Argumentum ad hominem* (appeal to their own practice).** Jesus uses a *qal wahomer* (light-to-heavy) argument, as in vv. 5–6. Even the strictest Pharisees would rescue their livestock on the Sabbath — an act the Talmud discusses but does not forbid (some said to feed the animal in the pit until the Sabbath ended, but practical need overrode that). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm; Constable via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/matthew-12.html)

- **Gill notes later rabbinic rules tried to restrict this practice,** perhaps in reaction to Jesus' argument: "If a beast fall into a ditch, or a pool of water, if food can be given it, where it is, they feed it till the going out of the sabbath." This rule may have been developed to close the loophole Jesus exposed. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/12.htm)

- **The principle:** Jesus establishes that it is always lawful "to do good" on the Sabbath. Mark's account (3:4) adds the penetrating alternative: "Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do evil, to save life or to kill?" Not to do good when it lies in one's power is, practically, to do evil. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

---

## v. 13 — *Then Jesus said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” So he stretched it out, and it was restored to full use, just like the other.*

- **An impossible command — requiring faith.** The man could not stretch out his withered hand by his own power. Jesus gave the command *and* the ability to fulfill it simultaneously. The man's obedience — stretching forth what he could not stretch forth — was itself an act of faith. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

- **Healed with a word, not touch.** Unlike other healings, Jesus used no physical ceremony here — demonstrating that His power does not depend on any ritual. "Christ sometimes used the ceremony of laying on his hand; here he doth not, to let us know that that was but a sign of what was done by his power." (Poole, cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

- **Mark adds Jesus' emotional response:** He "looked round about on them with anger, being grieved at the hardness of their hearts" (Mark 3:5). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

---

## v. 14 — *But the Pharisees went out and plotted how they might kill Jesus.*

- **A decisive turning point.** Previously the Pharisees had merely found fault and questioned Jesus. Now they moved to plotting His death. Mark 3:6 adds that they enlisted the Herodians — normally political enemies — in their conspiracy. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

- **The irony:** The Pharisees, who were so scrupulous about Sabbath law, spent that Sabbath plotting murder. As Enduring Word asks: "Which was more a violation of the Sabbath: when Jesus healed a man, or when these hate-filled men plotted the murder of a godly Man?" (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

- **They would not kill merely for a Sabbath violation.** Constable notes that the Pharisees "would not have put someone to death simply because he broke one of their traditional laws. They wanted to kill Jesus because they understood Him to be making messianic claims that they rejected." (Constable via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/matthew-12.html)

---

## vv. 15–16 — *Aware of this, Jesus withdrew from that place. Large crowds followed Him, and He healed them all, warning them not to make Him known.*

- **Strategic withdrawal, not cowardice.** Jesus withdrew because the hour of final conflict had not yet come; He respected the Father's timing. He was giving a practical example of His own precept in Matthew 10:23: "When they persecute you in this city, flee to another." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

- **"He healed them all."** This is one of the few sweeping summaries in the Gospels where Jesus healed *all* who came. Matthew stresses that the press of the multitudes did not make Jesus impatient or angry; He responded with compassion. The determination of the crowd was evidence of faith. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

- **"Warning them not to make Him known."** Jesus avoided premature publicity that would hasten the final conflict. Spurgeon notes: "He came not to contend with cavillers, and therefore he withdrew himself from the scene of their perpetual disputations…To him popularity became a hindrance in his work, and he shunned it." (Spurgeon via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/library/charles-spurgeon/gospel-of-the-kingdom/35.html)

---

## vv. 17–18 — *This was to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah: “Here is My Servant, whom I have chosen, My beloved, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him, and He will proclaim justice to the nations.”*

- **The quotation: Isaiah 42:1–4.** This is the longest Old Testament quotation in Matthew. It introduces the "Servant of the LORD," a figure who is central to the latter part of Isaiah — sometimes representing Israel collectively, sometimes a solitary, suffering figure. Matthew identifies Jesus as that Servant in His fullest sense. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

- **"My Servant, whom I have chosen, My beloved."** The language closely echoes the words at Jesus' baptism ("This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased," Matthew 3:17). The connection would not be lost on Matthew's readers. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

- **"He will proclaim justice to the Gentiles."** Matthew, though writing for a Jewish audience, emphasizes that the Messiah's mission extends to the Gentiles. Ellicott calls this "one of the many instances in which his record, though obviously written for Jews, is yet emphatically a Gospel for the Gentiles." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

---

## v. 19 — *“He will not quarrel or cry out; no one will hear His voice in the streets.”*

- **Gentleness, not weakness.** This does not mean Jesus never raised His voice (He did, in the temple cleansing and in His woes against the Pharisees). It describes His characteristic manner: He did not make His way by bluster, political agitation, or overpowering noise. His was a ministry of quiet authority — a stark contrast to the wrangling of scribes, the violence of Roman officials, and the revolutionary fervour of messianic pretenders like Judas the Galilean. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

- **Connected to the withdrawal and secrecy of vv. 15–16.** Jesus' avoidance of publicity fulfills this prophecy: He did not seek to create a public uproar or a political movement. (Spurgeon via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/library/charles-spurgeon/gospel-of-the-kingdom/35.html)

---

## v. 20 — *“A bruised reed He will not break, and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish, till He leads justice to victory.”*

- **Two tender images.** The "bruised reed" pictures a person broken by sorrow, care, or sin — someone others would disregard or trample. The "smoking flax" (or "dimly burning wick") pictures a soul whose light has nearly gone out, clogged by base desires, no longer burning brightly. Christ does not discard such persons. He "sought, if it were possible, to trim the lamp and to pour in the oil till the flame was bright again." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

- **The contrast with the Pharisees.** The self-righteous Pharisee had no pity for the bruised reed or smoking wick — he simply gave thanks that his own lamp was burning. Jesus is the opposite. Ellicott adds a personal touch: "We cannot help feeling, as we read the words, that the publican-apostle [Matthew] had found their fulfilment in his own personal experience of the profound tenderness of his Master." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

- **Spurgeon's pastoral reading:** "The feeblest are not disdained by our Lord Jesus, though apparently useless as a bruised reed, or even actually offensive as a smoking flax. He is gentle, and exercises no harsh severity. He bears and forbears with those who are unlovely in his eyes. He longs to bind up the broken reed, and fan the smoking flax into flaming life." (Spurgeon via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/library/charles-spurgeon/gospel-of-the-kingdom/35.html)

- **"Till He leads justice to victory."** The Hebrew of Isaiah reads "unto truth." Both readings convey that Christ's gentle, quiet work will persist until final judgment, when truth and justice ultimately triumph. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm; Pulpit Commentary via BibleHub: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/12-20.htm)

- **A different nuance from Desiring God (Reformed Baptist):** In its immediate context, the "unbreaking of bruised reeds" had to do with Jesus' need for secrecy — "He had to bring forth justice, but for a time, he also had to leave no trace of it." The conspiring Pharisees must not track Him too soon. (Desiring God: https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/gentle-jesus-and-the-compassion-conspiracy)

---

## v. 21 — *“In His name the nations will put their hope.”*

- **Isaiah's prophecy of Gentile inclusion.** The Hebrew text reads "in his law" (or "his teaching"), but Matthew follows the Septuagint reading "in his name." That the Gentiles would trust in the Jewish Messiah was both surprising and, for some of Matthew's readers, offensive — yet it was plainly Scriptural. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

- Spurgeon applies it personally: "Shall we not more and more trust in the Anointed of the Lord? Yes, Gentiles as we are, we do trust in his name. In us is this prophecy fulfilled." (Spurgeon via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/library/charles-spurgeon/gospel-of-the-kingdom/35.html)

---

## v. 22 — *Then a demon-possessed man who was blind and mute was brought to Jesus, and He healed the man so that he could speak and see.*

- **A triple affliction.** The man was demon-possessed, blind, and unable to speak. Unlike natural blindness or muteness, this was caused by demonic oppression. Calvin notes that Satan was permitted to injure the man's bodily senses: "We need not wonder that so much liberty should be allowed to Satan in injuring the bodily senses, when God justly permits him to corrupt or pervert all the faculties of the soul." (Calvin via CCEL: https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom32/calcom32.ii.xii.html)

- **A particularly difficult exorcism.** Lange calls this "the most difficult miracle" — to relieve one so fearfully under the power of the enemy, especially as the Pharisees watched "with unbelief and in bitterness of heart." (Lange via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/matthew-12.html)

- **This is not the same miracle as Matthew 9:32–33** (where a mute demoniac was healed), though Ellicott notes the charge was probably repeated on multiple occasions and answered similarly. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

---

## v. 23 — *The crowds were astounded and asked, “Could this be the Son of David?”*

- **"Son of David" = Messiah.** This was the most popular Messianic title among the people. The question in Greek is phrased to show uncertainty: "This couldn't be the Son of David, could it?" The people were moving toward faith but not yet fully convinced, despite seeing the fulfillment of Isaiah 35:5 ("Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped"). (Bible.org: https://new.bible.org/seriespage/18-beelzebub-or-holy-spirit-matthew-1222-37; Barnes via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/12-22.html)

- **The crowd's reaction versus the Pharisees'.** Lange notes: "The people were here on the point of openly proclaiming Jesus as the Son of David, or the Messiah. But they were prevented by the hierarchical party, who now came forward with their blasphemous accusation." (Lange via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/matthew-12.html)

- **Calvin:** "Acknowledging the power of God, they are led, as it were by the hand, to faith. Not that they suddenly profited as much as they ought to have done…but yet it is no small proficiency to be aroused to consider more attentively the glory of Christ." (Calvin via CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol32/htm/xiii.htm)

---

## v. 24 — *But when the Pharisees heard this, they said, “Only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, does this man drive out demons.”*

- **The name "Beelzebul" (or Beelzebub).** The name likely derives from *Baal-zebub* ("lord of the flies"), the Philistine god of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2), or possibly from *Baal-zebul* ("prince Baal"). It had become a Jewish designation for Satan, the prince of demons. Matthew identifies the two: "Beelzebul, the prince of demons." (Bible.org: https://new.bible.org/seriespage/18-beelzebub-or-holy-spirit-matthew-1222-37; France, cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

- **A charge of sorcery.** France notes: "The Pharisees' accusation amounts to a charge of sorcery, one which continued to be leveled against Jesus in later Jewish polemic." The charge is significant because it concedes the reality of Jesus' power — the Pharisees could not deny the miracle, so they had to attribute it to an evil source. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

- **Ellicott:** The words were "whispered by the Pharisees among the people. They were not addressed to Jesus." Jesus, however, knew their thoughts (v. 25). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

---

## v. 25 — *Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and every city or household divided against itself will not stand.”*

- **Jesus knew their thoughts.** This could be a mark of His divine omniscience, or a supernatural "word of knowledge" given by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:8). Ellicott calls Him "the Searcher of Hearts." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm)

- **The logic of a divided kingdom.** Jesus begins a multi-part refutation by appealing to common sense: no kingdom, city, or household can survive civil war. Satan's kingdom operates with a "distinct unity of purpose." If Satan were casting out his own agents, he would be working against himself — self-destructive behaviour that no rational being, however evil, would pursue. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/12.htm; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

- **A pointed observation.** As Bruce says: "Satan may be wicked, He says in effect, but he is not a fool." Spurgeon adds: "Whatever fault the devils have, they are not at strife with each other; that fault is reserved for the servants of a better Master." (Both cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

- **Matthew Poole:** "One devil may yield and give place to another, to gain a greater advantage for the whole society, but one never quarrelleth with another." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

---

## Summary of Denominational Distinctives

**Reformed (Calvin):** Stresses that Jesus did not erase the Sabbath but reoriented it around Himself. In v. 8, Calvin connects "Lord of the Sabbath" to the believer's freedom from the "bondage of the Law" — "out of Christ the bondage of the Law is wretched, from which he alone delivers those on whom he bestows the free Spirit of adoption." (Calvin via CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/study/Matthew_12:1-8)

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** Emphasises the poverty of Christ, His gentleness toward the weak ("bruised reed…smoking flax"), and the evangelistic application to Gentiles. Spurgeon reads v. 21 personally as fulfilled in Gentile believers. He also stresses the hardness of the Pharisees' hearts evident even in their plotting murder on the Sabbath. (Spurgeon via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/library/charles-spurgeon/gospel-of-the-kingdom/35.html)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/David Guzik):** Highlights Jesus' authority over demons (v. 22), the "binding of the strong man" as a principle for spiritual warfare (v. 29), and the ministry of the Holy Spirit — Jesus "honored the Spirit of God, and worked by his energy" (on v. 28). Guzik notes that the "word of knowledge" gift may explain Jesus knowing the Pharisees' thoughts in v. 25. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/)

**Lutheran:** The search results did not yield detailed Lutheran-specific commentary on this passage within the available sources. Lutherans would typically emphasise the distinction between Law and Gospel, seeing v. 8 as Christ's lordship freeing consciences from man-made Sabbath regulations while upholding the Sabbath's true purpose as a gift for rest and worship.

**Catholic/Orthodox:** No specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary was retrieved within the search/fetch limits for this passage. Catholic tradition (as seen in the Catena Aurea, which compiles patristic comments) and Orthodox tradition (as seen at oca.org) typically read these healing narratives as demonstrating Christ's divine authority and the principle that mercy supersedes ritual law — a reading broadly shared with Protestant traditions.

**Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes):** The NET Bible notes discuss the "sacred bread" (showbread) as the "bread of the Presence," twelve loaves prepared weekly (Exodus 25:30; Leviticus 24:5–9). On Jesus' defense, the notes observe: "Jesus is clear that on the surface there was a violation here. What is not as clear is whether he is arguing a 'greater need' makes this permissible or that this was within the intention of the law all along." (NET Bible via https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Mat+12%3A1-8)
